intro: Squamish sits at the head of Howe Sound in British Columbia, on the Sea-to-Sky Highway between Vancouver and Whistler. Just south of town, on the picnic lawn of Shannon Falls Provincial Park, stands a western red cedar whose trunk opens at the foot into a hollow a child could walk through. A reader photographed it and sent it to us; we do not yet know its age or girth.

question_answer: The Hollow Cedar of Shannon Falls is a western red cedar on the picnic lawn of Shannon Falls Provincial Park, just south of Squamish on the Sea-to-Sky Highway. It is free to see in the park's day-use area.
question_context: A reader sent us this tree from the picnic lawn at Shannon Falls, the provincial park just south of Squamish on the Sea-to-Sky Highway, with a note that the base of the tree is hollow and a child can walk through it. The photograph shows a western red cedar, Thuja plicata, standing on its own in the mown grass beside a paved path and a few picnic tables. Its trunk flares out at the foot into thick ribbed buttresses that part around a dark opening at ground level, and above the hollow it carries on straight and whole, its bark in long grey and red-brown strips, into a dense, drooping crown that rises well above the forest behind. Old western red cedars often go hollow at the heart while the outer wood keeps growing. We have no age, girth or height for this one; a reader who has measured it can tell us on the tree's page. The park is a day-use area with a car park, and the cedar stands on the lawn near the start of the trail to the falls.

trees.story:
"The base of the tree is hollow - a child can walk through it," wrote the reader who sent us this western red cedar from the picnic lawn at Shannon Falls, just south of Squamish on the Sea-to-Sky Highway.

The photograph shows what they mean. The cedar stands on its own in the mown grass, and its trunk flares out at the bottom into thick ribbed buttresses that part around a dark opening at ground level, tall enough to look into from the path. Above the hollow the trunk carries on straight and whole, its bark in long grey and red-brown strips, into a dense, drooping crown that rises far above the picnic tables and the forest of younger cedars behind.

Western red cedar is the great tree of the Pacific Northwest coast, and old ones often go hollow at the heart while the living wood around the outside keeps growing. A tree standing on an open hollow like this has had a long time to get there, but we have no age, girth or height for this one. If you know its story, or have measured it, tell us here and we will add it with your figures.

Come for the falls, which give the park its name, and stop at the cedar on the way back to the car park.
